title: Set Cover conjecture
formal:
Is the Set Cover conjecture true? For every \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), does there exist a fixed integer \(d\ge1\) such that no uniform randomized bounded-error algorithm solves \(\le d\)-Set Cover on an \(n\)-element universe in worst-case time
\[O\!\left((2-\varepsilon)^n(n+1)^r\right)\]
for any fixed exponent \(r\)? An instance supplies a family \(\mathcal F\subseteq2^{[n]}\) with \(|S|\le d\) for every \(S\in\mathcal F\), and an integer \(t\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\). The task is to decide whether some subfamily \(\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal F\) of at most \(t\) sets satisfies \(\bigcup_{S\in\mathcal H}S=[n]\). Sets chosen for the cover may overlap. The randomized interpretation is explicit in the later primary sources.
why: Set Cover is a central example of an exact algorithm whose natural dynamic-programming base remains two. The conjecture provides barriers for other exponential-time problems and is not merely a restatement of the familiar SAT hypotheses. Its incompatibility with the asymptotic rank conjecture links this algorithmic barrier to fundamental questions in algebraic complexity.
status_note: The 2024 SCC formulation and both STOC 2024 asymptotic-rank connections were checked on 2026-09-14, together with a bounded later-work search. The rank-based algorithms are conditional; no unconditional proof or refutation of the selected randomized SCC was identified.
review_note: Completed individual review against P versus NP on 2026-09-14; see research/card-completion-20260913/reviews.jsonl.

progress.text: Cygan and coauthors develop Set Cover-based lower bounds for exact exponential-time algorithms, keeping this assumption separate from the proved SAT equivalences.
Can Esmer and coauthors formulate the at-most-d Set Cover conjecture and characterize corresponding barriers for triangle partitioning and packing with structural parameters.
Björklund and Kaski show that the asymptotic rank conjecture and SCC cannot both hold.
Pratt improves the conditional Set Cover exponential base to arbitrarily close to 3/2^{2/3}, still assuming the asymptotic rank conjecture.

sentences: Set Cover asks whether a few supplied sets can cover a given universe.
The conjecture concerns exact algorithms when each available set has a fixed maximum size.
It says that no constant improvement over exponential base two works across all such size bounds.
The target allows bounded-error randomization and polynomial factors that depend on the fixed bound.
Recent results show that a major conjecture about tensor rank would refute SCC, but neither side is settled unconditionally.

definitions:
Let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge1\). Each set is represented by its sorted list of distinct element indices in binary; the family is an explicitly supplied list without duplicate sets. Empty sets and an empty family are allowed. Write \(m=|\mathcal F|\). For fixed \(d\),
\[m\le\sum_{j=0}^{\min(d,n)}\binom nj\le(n+1)^d,\]
so the entire valid input has length polynomial in \(n\), with its degree allowed to depend on \(d\). The threshold can be capped at \(n\), since any cover contains a subcover of at most \(n\) sets. The question counts the universe size, not the number of available sets or selected sets, in the exponential part of the time bound.

Use a uniform random-access machine with finite program, binary words of length \(w=\lceil4(n+\log_2(m+2)+1)\rceil\), and word-addressed memory. This allows the usual exponential-size dynamic-programming tables while keeping each word polynomially many bits long. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copies, branches, comparisons, addition/subtraction/multiplication modulo \(2^w\), integer division with remainder by a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, shifts, and obtaining a uniformly random independent word. Shifts by at least \(w\) and division by zero may return zero. Initially memory holds only the input and otherwise zeroes. Every table construction and preprocessing operation is counted. The machine has no oracle or nonuniform advice, and no operation acts on an exponentially long bit string as one word. Charging polynomial bit cost for scalar word operations only alters the allowed polynomial factor.

A randomized algorithm must return the correct decision with probability at least \(2/3\) on every valid input and halt within its asserted time bound on every random tape. The bound means that for a fixed \(d,\varepsilon\), there are constants \(K,r,n_0\) for which runtime is at most \(K(2-\varepsilon)^n(n+1)^r\) whenever \(n\ge n_0\). All finite smaller valid instances must also be correctly decided. These constants and the program may depend on \(d,\varepsilon\), but not on \(n,\mathcal F,t\).

The negation is a single \(\varepsilon>0\) that works for every fixed \(d\), allowing a different algorithm and polynomial factor for each \(d\). An improved base for one particular set-size bound does not refute the conjecture. The decision version used here and the source's minimum-cover optimization version have the same exponential base: searching thresholds and recovering a cover uses only polynomially many calls for fixed \(d\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the conjecture or its negation in the stated randomized computational model. A refutation must give a uniform positive improvement of the exponential base across every fixed maximum set size. Proving a lower bound assuming SETH or another conjecture, restricting to deterministic algorithms, improving one bounded-size case, or counting only arithmetic operations on unbounded-size objects does not settle this target.

context_blocks.text: A subset dynamic program solves the problem in \(2^n\operatorname{poly}(n,m)\) time. The target asks whether the base two can be reduced by a constant independent of the maximum allowed set size. Polynomial factors are explicitly permitted and may grow with that fixed size bound.

The family is given explicitly and each set has at most d elements. This is distinct from requiring exactly d elements, requiring a partition into disjoint sets, or bounding how many sets contain each element. The 2024 source studies reductions between such variants, but the card fixes the at-most-d covering version.

Cygan and coauthors use the Set Cover assumption for tight conditional bounds on several exact algorithms. Their work does not prove that the ordinary Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis implies this Set Cover conjecture.

Björklund and Kaski prove that Strassen’s asymptotic rank conjecture would yield a randomized sub-two-base algorithm and hence refute SCC. Pratt strengthens the conditional algorithm. These are incompatibility and conditional-algorithm theorems, not unconditional resolutions of either conjecture.
